title: Their opinion, strangely
hook: we love ourselves most but trust others' opinion of us more than our own (Meditations 12.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: now, if you want it. Your line was now, not later. What did you stop postponing? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

You've decided the outfit looks good. Then someone glances at it a certain way, and suddenly it doesn't. You were sure the idea was solid, until a coworker raised one eyebrow. It's odd. We spend every waking minute with ourselves, know our own reasons better than anyone, and still hand the verdict to whoever happens to be looking. Marcus noticed the same oddness, and wrote it down as a puzzle. Today: their opinion, strangely.
screen: `THE OUTFIT, AND THE GLANCE.` → `ONE RAISED EYEBROW.` → `THEIR OPINION, STRANGELY.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. I've often wondered, Marcus writes, how it is that every person loves himself more than anyone else, and yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on other people's opinion of him. Second, the test. Then he proposes a thought experiment. Suppose a god, or a wise teacher, stood beside you and told you never to think anything you wouldn't say out loud the moment you thought it. Nobody could bear it, he says, not even for a single day. Third, what that shows. So we're more concerned with what our neighbors will think of us than with what we think of ourselves. We guard the outside carefully and leave the inside to anyone. We'll rewrite an email five times for how it sounds, and let a mean thought run all morning unchecked. Fourth, turning it around. Marcus isn't saying other people's views never matter; a friend's honest criticism can be a gift. He's pointing at a strange imbalance. The one person who's with you every minute, who knows your reasons and your efforts, gets the smallest vote. Today's practice gives that person, you, a little more say: look honestly, decide, and let your own judgment stand without checking the room first.
screen: `LOVE OURSELVES, TRUST THEM MORE.` · `SAY EVERY THOUGHT ALOUD?` · `WE GUARD THE OUTSIDE.` · `GIVE YOURSELF A VOTE.` · then, large: `MY OWN OPINION.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of a choice you've been second-guessing because of what someone might think: a plan, a purchase, the way you dress, a thing you want to say. Set their imagined opinion aside for a moment. Ask yourself honestly: what do I think? Is it reasonable? Is it kind? If the answer is yes, decide to trust it, just this once, without asking anyone to approve it first. Notice how that feels, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Their opinion. Marcus's puzzle: we love ourselves most, yet value other people's opinion of us more than our own. Today's word.
Your line: my own opinion. Make one decision today on your own honest judgment, and don't check the room before you act. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: People who draw on this passage sometimes pause before seeking reassurance and first ask what they themselves honestly think, then act on it when it's reasonable and kind.

fork.setup: a god stands beside you and says: from now on, say every thought aloud as soon as you think it. what does Marcus think you'd do?
fork.reveal: nobody could bear it even for a day, he writes, which shows we care more about what neighbors think of us than what we think of ourselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't care what people think.
what it means: we give everyone a bigger vote on ourselves than we give ourselves; Marcus asks why.
what a scholar hears: the entry ends on the neighbors: we pay more respect to what they'll think of us than to what we think of ourselves.

notes: 12.4 paraphrased (Long: 'I have often wondered how it is that every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others. If then a god or a wise teacher should present himself to a man and bid him to think of nothing and to design nothing which he would not express as soon as he conceived it, he could not endure it even for a single day. So much more respect have we to what our neighbours shall think of us than to what we shall think of ourselves.'). Confirm.
